content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a unique (to this reviewer) take on testing the behavior of V&L models. The main idea behind the paper is to use the named semantic properties of objects as identified by humans (dog is furry, dog is mammal, dog barks, etc..) and use them to probe both representation aspects of a model as well as how similarly these models process/perceive these entities compared to humans. The experiments are done on a set of popular and diverse types of recent V&L models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

*[S1]:* A new take on behavioral analysis of VL models: This provides a new way to look at what the model learns (representation)  in terms of identification of whether a concept (object) possesses certain properties (features) and how they shape a model's decisions. Furthermore, by making an explicit connection with human psycholinguistic characteristics in how people tend to label these features for concepts, the paper presents the possibility of an entirely new way to understand model decisions in reference to human understanding of the world. 

*[S2]:* A nice and wide variety of models tested: The models tested are well-known, state-of-the-art in their own turf models that should provide more than enough variety to do any behavioral study of recent V&L models. I have no complaints or desire to see more models compared to here. 

**Weaknesses** 

*[W1]*: Severe issues with clarity and details: To this reviewer, the writing is opaque, hard to parse, and poorly organized. Here is the list of questions that I would like some clarity on. They range from "I think I mostly got it through enough repetitions and context, thought it was never made fully clear in the text" to "I have no idea". 

W1.1: "Concepts" are ImageNet objects that overlap with entities mentioned in McRae feature norms; and "features" are McRae semantic properties of those said objects. Is that correct? Does "feature type" means one of the properties from McRae? Or are they the "meta-group" that they belong to? (e.g., taxonomic information, etc..)? 

W1.2: On page 4, 
> For every semantic feature type t (e.g., taxonomic, visuo-perceptual) we select the corresponding feature set (columns), compute the cosine distance (eq. 1) between every pair of concepts (rows), and concatenate them into a vector u_t. . For every pair of different feature sets ti, tj we have ti ∩ tj = ∅. 

Firstly, are there an equal number of annotation per feature? Otherwise, since each column represents the number of people that consider object "Concept" to have a property "feature", I am not sure if the cosine similarity is meaningful. Next, how is "the cosine distance (eq. 1) between every pair of concepts" computed for each column separately? This is just a single thing, how is this different "per column"? Then, why does the vector u_t represent the feature for the feature type t? I am not sure I understand the idea behind the "concatenation of cosine similarity of all pairs of an object (row)" as being the feature for a given feature. And finally, what are ti and tj? If this is defined somewhere I missed it! 

W.1.3: Since I do not understand W.1.2, a *LOT* of the paper is unclear. Later the ut above is mentioned as the "semantic vector" I don't understand how :( 

W1.3: At several points in the paper, there is a study of "per-layer" feature interaction. Why is this done?

W.1.4 The unimodal counterpart for both CLIP and ViLT is VIT-B/32. Why does the uvis result have different numbers for similarity in Figure 2 for CLIP and VILT? Since the unimodal counterpart have nothing to do with VILT or CLIP, shouldn't they be the same?

W1.5 When the paper refers to "the image and text streams", is it talking about a single vector representation of image and text, or actually a "sequence"? If latter, I do not believe the CLIP "streams" are encoding anything. Since the only real representation learning happens at the [CLS] token, the other time-steps are useless (at least in the final layer) and hold no information. Indeed, the loss does not even even affect those outputs. 


*[W2]*: Suboptimal test setup for the methods tested: Due to W1 above, it is quite hard to understand what exactly is the test setup for each of the models tested but it sounds like the input to the models are *single* words. For both ALBEF and CLIP, this is quite a sub-optimal setup. Even for a single concept (dog), CLIP recommends the use of a prompt (if not an average of many prompts, as done for ZS imagenet evaluation). Similarly, to compute image-text similarity, ALBEF and ViLT would fare better if the model finetuned on text-image retrieval is used rather than image-text matching, which is considered a "pre-training" stage/target. At this point, the model has only been trained on masked language, which degrades its ability to truly match with the whole query; While it is still decent, I would consider this a sub-optimal setup. Finally, the use of a single-image occupying the whole canvas setup of ImageNet is also something I consider "outside of normal expected usage" for ALBEF and ViLT, which focuses more on complex scenes with many objects and their description. 

*[W3]*: No attempt to avoid, address or discuss potentially confounding factors-- The methods being tested are *VERY* different in terms of how they are trained and what they attempt to do well. This would normally be a great thing as it would show model behaviors for a wide range of techniques. However, it also makes the head-to-head comparison poor (as the paper has done in several places). For example, there is a *HUGE* amount of difference in how much data CLIP uses compared to ALBEF. It is generally understood that methods that employ some form of cross-attention processing learn better image-text alignment in the small-data regime (e.g., ALBEF does better on image retrieval despite using ~100x fewer data points). It is not clear how big of an impact this makes in the tests that are conducted. Similarly, due to the nature of training, they all have different strengths. E.g., CLIP can be expected to have much higher vocabulary exposure compared to ALBEF, how does this affect the tests?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** To me, it is very poor; I spent many hours and am still not very certain I have a good grasp of what is being measured with the tests and why they work/do not work. See W1 above

**Quality:** See strengths and weaknesses above.

**Novelty:** It is quite new and exciting! 

**Reproducibility:** Due to clarity, I feel the reproducibility is poor. To this reviewer, reproducibility means more than being able to run a command in a provided git repo (which the authors have promised to do) but being able to understand and independently reproduce the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a refreshingly new take on studying and explaining model behaviors. However, it is held back by severe clarity issues and what I perceive to be sub-optimal test setups, where the reasons for the observed differences may be explained by other spurious factors such as model training data, its expected usage pattern etc... However, lack of clarity is the bigger reason for my score. I do recognize that "lack of clarity" is subjective and if I differ from my fellow reviewers and if the authors address my questions well, I am open to trying harder to understand the paper and thus raising my scores.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to reviewer 6tzB - Part 1
content.comment:
We thank reviewer 6tzB for their thorough revision of our work. For our next version of the manuscript, we will work on improving its clarity taking into account the points mentioned by the reviewer. We now address their questions as follows:

> W1.1: "Concepts" are ImageNet objects that overlap with entities mentioned in McRae feature norms; and "features" are McRae semantic properties of those said objects. Is that correct? Does "feature type" means one of the properties from McRae? Or are they the "meta-group" that they belong to? (e.g., taxonomic information, etc..)?

The definition of  “Concepts” and “Features” of reviewer 6tzB are correct. “Feature types” refer to the “meta-groups” that the features belong to depending on the type of information they are conveying. That is, a feature is associated with a specific feature type that could be one of: 1) taxonomic, 2) visual-perceptual, 3) perceptual non-visual, 4) functional, 5) encyclopaedic.

In the next version of our manuscript, we will clarify the distinction between “concepts”, “features” and “feature types” more thoroughly.

> W1.2: On page 4, For every semantic feature type t (e.g., taxonomic, visuo-perceptual) we select the corresponding feature set (columns), compute the cosine distance (eq. 1) between every pair of concepts (rows), and concatenate them into a vector u_t. . For every pair of different feature sets ti, tj we have ti ∩ tj = ∅. Firstly, are there an equal number of annotation per feature? Otherwise, since each column represents the number of people that consider object "Concept" to have a property "feature", I am not sure if the cosine similarity is meaningful. Next, how is "the cosine distance (eq. 1) between every pair of concepts" computed for each column separately? This is just a single thing, how is this different "per column"? Then, why does the vector u_t represent the feature for the feature type t? I am not sure I understand the idea behind the "concatenation of cosine similarity of all pairs of an object (row)" as being the feature for a given feature. And finally, what are ti and tj? If this is defined somewhere I missed it!

> W.1.3: Since I do not understand W.1.2, a LOT of the paper is unclear. Later the ut above is mentioned as the "semantic vector" I don't understand how :(

We thank the reviewer for bringing up this source of confusion. We will try to explain the experimental set-up in a different manner for a (hopefully) clearer understanding. Let us define $M$ as an $|\mathcal{C}| \times \mathcal{|F|}$ matrix, where $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of concepts and $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of features. In this matrix, $m_{ij}$ represents the number of people that when asked about the properties of concept $i$, named the feature $j$. Let us now define $\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{F}$ where $\mathcal{U}$ is the subset of features that belong to a determined feature type $t$ (e.g. taxonomic features). We can now reduce our matrix $M$ to be of dimensions $|\mathcal{C}| \times |\mathcal{U}|$, and compute the pairwise cosine distances between the concept rows. The result of each pairwise comparison is a scalar number representing the distance between two concept if we only represent them using the properties of a specific feature-type. To give an example, the concept "zuchinni" and "alligator" might be taxonomically very different (when is a reptile, another is a vegetable), but visually more similar (both are green and long). We then concatenate all these scalar distances into a vector $\mathbb{u}_t$ that we call the "semantic vector" because it represents the distances between concepts defined by their semantic properties (in other words, because the columns of these vectors are representing semantic properties).

We hope this new explanation helped clarify this part of our experimental set-up. In our next version of the manuscript, we will improve the use of notations, add more intuitive explanations of the analysis, and include figures of the metrics to aid interpretation.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6tzB - Part 2
content.comment:
> W1.3: At several points in the paper, there is a study of "per-layer" feature interaction. Why is this done?

There were two main ways in which we carried out per-layer analysis. First, we compared the representational spaces of each pair of layers of V+L models and those of their unimodal counterparts (shown in Figure 1 of Supplementary Material). This analysis was carried out to test that indeed multimodal training changes the distances learned between concepts.

We also used per-layer analysis to compare how similar the conceptual behavior of V+L models is to the conceptual representations of unimodal models. More specifically, we extracted the conceptual representations of each layer of the unimodal models and compare them to the conceptual behavior of V+L models, to test if the concept predictions of the multi-modal models are aligned to different stages of conceptual representations in a unimodal network. To give an example, it could be the case that the invariances learned at the first layers of vision models to discriminate two concepts are too “visually specific” to resemble those used by V+L models to make predictions.

> W.1.4 The unimodal counterpart for both CLIP and ViLT is VIT-B/32. Why does the uvis result have different numbers for similarity in Figure 2 for CLIP and VILT? Since the unimodal counterpart have nothing to do with VILT or CLIP, shouldn't they be the same?

Figure 2 shows the similarity between the conceptual behavior of each model with that of their unimodal counterpart. As reviewer 6tzB pointed out,  the visual counterpart of CLIP and ViLT is the same. However, in the first subplot we are correlating the concept predictions of CLIP with the conceptual space of VIT-B/32, while in the second subplot we are correlating the concept predictions of ViLT with the conceptual space of VIT-B/32. We will better clarify this comparison in our next version of the manuscript.

> W1.5 When the paper refers to "the image and text streams", is it talking about a single vector representation of image and text, or actually a "sequence"? If latter, I do not believe the CLIP "streams" are encoding anything. Since the only real representation learning happens at the [CLS] token, the other time-steps are useless (at least in the final layer) and hold no information. Indeed, the loss does not even even affect those outputs.

The word stream is used to denote a single vector representation. As stated on page 4 first paragraph, we extracted the representations of the [CLS] or [EOS] tokens of each stream to investigate the conceptual spaces of the DNNs.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer 6tzB - Part 2

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6tzB - Part 3
content.comment:
> [W2]: Suboptimal test setup for the methods tested: Due to W1 above, it is quite hard to understand what exactly is the test setup for each of the models tested but it sounds like the input to the models are single words. For both ALBEF and CLIP, this is quite a sub-optimal setup. Even for a single concept (dog), CLIP recommends the use of a prompt (if not an average of many prompts, as done for ZS imagenet evaluation). Similarly, to compute image-text similarity, ALBEF and ViLT would fare better if the model finetuned on text-image retrieval is used rather than image-text matching, which is considered a "pre-training" stage/target. At this point, the model has only been trained on masked language, which degrades its ability to truly match with the whole query; While it is still decent, I would consider this a sub-optimal setup. Finally, the use of a single-image occupying the whole canvas setup of ImageNet is also something I consider "outside of normal expected usage" for ALBEF and ViLT, which focuses more on complex scenes with many objects and their description.

We thank the reviewer for their suggestions on improving our test setup. We will take these into account.

Regarding prompt usage, we want to point out that we did not carry out prompt engineering in the current work because the concept detection accuracies that we achieved using single words were already very high. In any case, our aim was not to achieve the best possible accuracy in concept detection but to examine the patterns of concept discrimination that should be observable even if the classification setup is not optimal. Moreover, for the case of the semantic-feature detection task, the prompts were not made up of single words, but phrases describing the semantic property, e.g. “is made of wood”. However, we agree with the reviewer that we should control that our effects are not dependent on the prompt used, and we will add this analysis to our next version of the manuscript.

Regarding the fine-tuned models, we did actually use image-text fine-tuned models using the COCO dataset for ALBEF and ViLT. We realize that we have forgotten to include this information in our manuscript, and we will thus include it in the next version.

Regarding the image set-up, we want to point out that the images composing the THINGS dataset are extracted from ImageNet, so although their simple nature is not a frequent characteristic in large image datasets, they are still part of common training setups. In addition, we also considered using more complex images in previous versions of this work, but this made it really difficult to evaluate the accuracy of the semantic feature detection task. This is because even in the most densely annotated complex image datasets like Visual Genome, we found that almost all images missed annotating some object. This impacts how accurately we could measure that the semantic predictions of a model are correct. For example, if the image contained a cat in the background that was not annotated in the dataset, the model might still produce a high score for a semantic feature like “is an animal”, while our ground truth was missing such possibility. Since we found that concepts could be accurately detected using these simpler images, we decided this was the cleaner setup for our experiment.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer 6tzB - Part 3

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6tzB - Part 4
content.comment:
> [W3]: No attempt to avoid, address or discuss potentially confounding factors-- The methods being tested are VERY different in terms of how they are trained and what they attempt to do well. This would normally be a great thing as it would show model behaviors for a wide range of techniques. However, it also makes the head-to-head comparison poor (as the paper has done in several places). For example, there is a HUGE amount of difference in how much data CLIP uses compared to ALBEF. It is generally understood that methods that employ some form of cross-attention processing learn better image-text alignment in the small-data regime (e.g., ALBEF does better on image retrieval despite using ~100x fewer data points). It is not clear how big of an impact this makes in the tests that are conducted. Similarly, due to the nature of training, they all have different strengths. E.g., CLIP can be expected to have much higher vocabulary exposure compared to ALBEF, how does this affect the tests?

We agree with the reviewer that we cannot make strong statements as to why the results between the V+L models differ. We can only hypothesize about the mechanisms driving these differences. We will include a more thorough discussion of the possibilities mentioned by the reviewers in our next version of the manuscript. 

Nonetheless, we want to point out that our aim was not to uncover the mechanisms driving the different conceptual behaviors of  V+L models, but rather 1) provide a diagnostic tool to easily characterize the conceptual behavior of any V+L model and  2) use our method to characterize the conceptual behavior and semantic knowledge of widely used V+L models, and show that they exhibit different behaviors that cannot be predicted from their classification accuracy,  Our central aim was thus not to measure how accurately these models predict concepts or semantic features, but rather characterize their patterns of conceptual and semantic mistakes, and explore the relationship between these two. 

In addition, it is worth noting that we found that the models with the highest accuracy like CLIP or ALBEF, exhibit a conceptual behavior that is less human-like than ViLT, which has more modest conceptual and semantic detection capabilities. So even if we would have expected better alignment for some of these models due to some of the confounding reasons mentioned by the reviewer (like the amount of training data), we found the opposite pattern. We will discuss this point in more detail in our next version of the manuscript.

Finally, we want to point out that we also tried to select V+L models that allow us to control for some hypothetically relevant factors. In particular, ALBEF and ViLT are trained on the same datasets, using very similar pre-training tasks (they only differ in the use of a momentum distillation loss), and using the same fine-tuning dataset. This reduces the possible reasons behind their differences.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors try to understand the differences in features that multimodal and a unimodal models learn across a set of tasks. The authors aggregate the pairwise features of models and construct correlations across a variety of tasks. They try to explain the features that humans pick up on using different multimodal and unimodal models and find that ViLT does a decent job sometimes of capturing similar correlations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The strength of this paper is that there are interesting results between human features and ViLT features across a variety of concepts. The paper doesn't provide any experiments that attempt to really understand what is going on though. Most of the explanations are hand-wavy and an attempt to interpret the correlations they see. An interesting follow-up experiment would be to see what the ViLT is attending to and whether this correlates appropriately to what humans look for.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Writing was pretty clear, but I am not sure how novel this work is. Can probably be reproduced easily but I don't see any github link.
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting results but not enough analysis to warrant ICLR acceptance.

content.title: Response to reviewer 2sq3
content.comment:
We thank reviewer 2sq3 for revising our manuscript. Below we address some of their comments:

> The paper doesn't provide any experiments that attempt to really understand what is going on though. Most of the explanations are hand-wavy and an attempt to interpret the correlations they see.

We agree that given the correlational nature of our study we cannot provide definite conclusions as to which mechanisms are driving the differences between the multimodal models. However, our aim was not to uncover the mechanisms driving the different conceptual behaviors of  V+L models, but rather 1) provide a diagnostic tool to easily characterize the conceptual behavior and semantic knowledge of any V+L model, and 2) use our method to show that widely used V+L models exhibit different conceptual behaviors, and these cannot be predicted from their classification accuracy. We will clarify these aims better in the next version of our paper.

> An interesting follow-up experiment would be to see what the ViLT is attending to and whether this correlates appropriately to what humans look for.

We appreciate reviewer 2sq3 suggestion of carrying out some follow-up analysis of ViLT’s processing mechanisms. We will include such an analysis in the next version of our manuscript.

> Writing was pretty clear, but I am not sure how novel this work is. Can probably be reproduced easily but I don't see any github link.

We did not include a github link to conform with the anonymity requirement. Instead, all our code was (and is) available in the zip file provided as supplementary material.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a suite of evaluation tests for studying the ability of vision and language models to match human reasoning with respect to concept understanding, including about hyponymy and attributes. They evaluate the proposed suite of metrics on several well-known vision-and-language models, and found that model performance on existing benchmarks does not necessarily correlate with similarity to human behavior. There are a few conclusions, e.g., that early-fusion based vision and language models may have better conceptual representation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Studying an important problem, and introducing a suite of evaluation could be useful for the community
- Thorough experiments

Weaknesses:
- My main concern is that the paper is actually quite difficult to follow. In Section 3.3, there is notation used that is never formally defined. I'd strongly suggest interleaving experimental results with the metric definitions, because otherwise it's very unclear how the metrics work in practice. I also strongly suggest visualizing the metrics somehow (not the metric results, but the metrics themselves; specifically, with examples of how the metrics are computed for particular image+text pairs).
- Similarly, I found the figures hard to understand, e.g., with axes that aren't defined (e.g., Figure 1 -- what are the two dimensions here? What is being plotted?)
- Choosing concepts from McRae may be somewhat limiting in the kind of concepts that are probed for in these evaluations. How lexically diverse is McRae? Did you consider using other sources of commonsense information about entities and their properties, such as ATOMIC, WordNet, etc?
- It was also unclear where the human judgments came from. Is that from the original McRae dataset? If so, did you consider collecting additional human judgments on the same data that was used in the experiments?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
- This is my biggest concern with the paper: I found it pretty hard to follow the numerous metrics and their results, especially without examples and with undefined notation.

Quality:
- The experiments appear thorough, although there is not a concrete conclusion to the findings (not necessarily a bad thing).

Originality:
- I haven't seen this thorough of a probing into model predictions, so I'd say this is a relatively new approach.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper addresses an important problem for understanding the behavior of vision-and-language models. While the experiments are thorough, I am concerned about the readability; in its current state the paper is hard to follow for a few reasons listed above.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4534 by Reviewer jNT9

content.title: Response to reviewer jNT9
content.comment:
We thank reviewer jNT9 for their valuable feedback. We appreciate their suggestions for improving the clarity of the paper. In the next version of the manuscript, we will: 1) Interleave the metric definition with the metric results; 2) Add a visual illustration of the metrics; 3) Improve the formal definition of the notations; 4) Improve the figures and its notations.

To answer the questions from reviewer jTN9:

> Figure 1 -- what are the two dimensions here? What is being plotted?

The plot shows the spearman correlation between the representational spaces of each pair of layers of a multimodal network and their unimodal counterpart. The representational spaces are constructed by taking the cosine distance between the layer activations of each pair of images. The label ticks of each axis represent the layers of the networks. We will make this clearer in the next version of this manuscript.

> How lexically diverse is McRae? Did you consider using other sources of commonsense information about entities and their properties, such as ATOMIC, WordNet, etc?

If defining lexical diversity as the ratio of different unique word stems to the total number of words, the McRae dataset has a lexical diversity of 23.7%.

We indeed tried other commonsense databases, specifically ConceptNet and WordNet. We decided against these databases since 1) the properties listed in ConceptNet are less defining of an entity than those of McRae, contain biases, and contain without differentiation the properties pertaining to all senses associated with the concept’s name (e.g. for the concept “bat” we found properties associated with the animal and with the object related to baseball); 2) the properties that could be extracted from WordNet were very few.

However, we agree that including another commonsense database would be important to investigate the generalizability of our results, and for the next version of our manuscript we will try to find an additional source of information.

> It was also unclear where the human judgments came from. Is that from the original McRae dataset? If so, did you consider collecting additional human judgments on the same data that was used in the experiments?

The human judgments linking a concept and a semantic property are taken from the McRae dataset. In this study, participants were asked to name features related to 541 concepts that were carefully chosen based on previous studies of semantic memory. Approximately 30 participants gave an answer for each concept, and only those features that more than 5 participants mentioned were included in the final database.

For the next version of our manuscript, we will consider including additional validations of the accuracy of the McRae dataset, and additional human judgments.
